ideas.who_does_it_today: DTN WeatherOps live-event services (no published price); National Weather Service decision support; University of Alabama in Huntsville lightning tool used at Rock the South; Beazley parametric rain product; independent event meteorologists.

ideas.title: Surcharge Clawback: tariff pass-through, contract-price and hidden-fee recovery for healthcare buyers
ideas.one_liner: Read two years of a provider's supplier invoices, find tariff surcharges, tariff-timed price steps and fee creep, match each to the contract clause that lets the buyer claim money back, and take 20% of what comes back.
ideas.customer: Owner or CFO of an owner-operated healthcare services company (MHC first), then other home-health agencies (about 12,200 Medicare-certified), DME suppliers (about 79,000 enrolled), labs and clinics.
ideas.who_pays: The provider pays 20% of net cash, credit or price reduction recovered; no recovery means no fee, so no budget line is needed. Later a roughly $2,000 a year ledger subscription.
ideas.problem: Buyers saw 'tariff surcharge' lines and quiet price increases in 2025. The Supreme Court ruled the IEEPA tariffs unlawful on Feb 20, 2026 (about $166B collected; refunds to importers of record via CBP's CAPE portal since Apr 20). Only the importer of record gets the refund; the buyer who paid gets nothing unless a surcharge, true-up or refund-sharing clause, or an unjust-enrichment theory, forces a share. Private disputes only surfaced in Sept 2026 and no court has decided pass-through claims on the merits. Most small buyers have not identified which invoice lines to claim.
ideas.solution: Ingest supplier invoices (PDF, email, CSV) into a ledger of every surcharge line and unit-price step; map suppliers to importer of record where known; quote the relevant contract clause and score claim strength; output an evidence pack plus a demand letter the client's own officer or counsel signs (he does not give legal advice). Same pass also checks contract/GPO price compliance and fee creep (fuel, environmental, regulatory, small-order, shipping and handling) in the pattern of the Stericycle case (class of 246,000+, $295M settlement, $608M alleged overcharges). Kill test first: two hours on 12 months of MHC's top-5 supply vendor invoices; if there are no surcharge lines, no tariff-month price steps and no fee creep, drop the tariff angle.
ideas.why_now: Refunds reached importers from April 2026 and supplier-buyer disputes began in September; the window where suppliers will still negotiate before positions harden is months. Law firms publish advice but nobody sells a low-ticket productized service to a 10-site home-health operator. Caveat: one firm says most serious refund seekers already have their money, so speed matters.
ideas.founder_edge: His mother works at MHC, so real invoices exist on day one; the freight engine already does 'billed line vs tariff or contract'; vendor invoices normally contain no PHI so no BAA in the first pass (strip patient identifiers if present); AI-speed ingestion and ledger building.
ideas.first_10_customers: 1) MHC itself (12 months of supplier invoices via his mother). 2-4) Two or three other agencies or DME shops the grandfather or MHC administrators name when asked who they trade notes with. 5) A pharmacy or clinic in the family circle. 6) Annapolis Baygrass (equipment rental and merch invoices). 7-10) Intros from the state home-care association and an HME buying group such as VGM (about 3,500 member providers). Get an attorney's written answer first on unauthorized practice of law, state collection licensing for a contingency fee on a commercial claim, and lawyer fee-splitting.
ideas.path_to_big: Honest: the tariff pool is one-time and the law is unsettled. It only becomes big as a recurring vendor surcharge ledger with a clause database: 5,000 customers at about $2,000 a year is $10M, a heroic share of roughly 91,000 agencies and DME suppliers unless it expands to clinics, dental, vet and senior living.
ideas.who_does_it_today: RSK Supplier Recovery (consulting-led, pricing unpublished); law-firm advisories (Jones Walker, Covington, Baker Donelson); importer-side tariff refund shops (Tariff Recovery Group and similar); carriers refunding their own duty payers (FedEx, UPS, DHL); home-care GPOs (HPSI, IMCO, MED Group with 3-5% stated savings); Cass waste expense management for large healthcare accounts. No self-serve ledger for small multi-site providers found.

ideas.title: MedFreight Desk: freight audit plus damage claims for medical-device and medical-supply makers and distributors
ideas.one_liner: Point the finished LTL and parcel audit engine at one vertical (companies that make or distribute medical products), add a damage-claims desk, and reach them through MHC's suppliers and the manufacturing-extension network.
ideas.customer: Owner or operations lead at a 5-100 person medical-device maker, supply importer or distributor, starting in Florida (26,000+ manufacturers, 80% with 20 or fewer employees; roughly 400-1,000+ device makers by inconsistent old counts).
ideas.who_pays: The manufacturer pays 15% of recovered overcharges (free first look) plus 20% on filed damage claims.
ideas.problem: LTL accessorials, reclass and reweigh bills go unaudited at small shippers. Medical products ship high value per pallet and are handling-sensitive, so damage claims are bigger. The NMFC density rewrite effective July 19, 2025 is still producing reclass bills. Carmack gives at least 9 months to file claims and the statute does not shift a claims firm's fee to the carrier.
ideas.solution: Run the existing engine (22 checks, 2,266 tests, 187 callable prospects) with a medical pack: documentation for damage and temperature claims, serial/lot traceability fields, a claims-filing desk for small claims big shops ignore. Offer a free first look, then 15% contingency.
ideas.why_now: Density-class change and rising LTL accessorials; FloridaMakes (official NIST MEP representative in Florida) and the Florida SBDC network have an MOU, so a ready-made advisor channel exists; the engine is finished and idle with zero calls made since August.
ideas.founder_edge: The engine, the call sheet and the site already exist; the only missing input is calls. His mother can ask MHC procurement to introduce three suppliers, a warm door a cold call lacks.
ideas.first_10_customers: Three suppliers MHC's purchasing contact introduces; three FloridaMakes or SBDC introductions (offer a short talk for small manufacturers); four from the existing call sheet filtered to medical products. Later other states' MEP centers.
ideas.path_to_big: Honest math: a maker with $200k of LTL spend and a 4% error rate yields $8,000 recoverable, or $1,200-1,600 a year at 15-20%, so $10M needs 6,000-8,000 clients. Only big with claims automation, the event-evidence data asset (idea 3) and the MEP channel across states. Prior validation scored the generic version 3.33/10; this changes the door and claims upside, not the ceiling.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Eller Audit (free first audit at 15%), the freight-audit-and-payment field (Cass, nVision and others), freight claims shops such as TLI, Warp's free reweigh/reclass and accessorial audit tools, vMeasure and FreightSizer for dimensions.

ideas.title: Event Truth: independent evidence that a billed freight event actually happened
ideas.one_liner: For every accessorial on a freight bill (liftgate, inside delivery, residential, limited access, redelivery), assemble independent evidence from licensed address data, a 20-second consignee text and the delivery receipt, and file the dispute with the evidence attached.
ideas.customer: Small shippers with repeat consignees: medical makers shipping to clinics, DME shops delivering to homes, small distributors; later freight-audit firms and brokers via API.
ideas.who_pays: The shipper pays 20% of accessorials recovered (bundled with MedFreight), later $2-5 per verified shipment; audit firms and brokers pay per-shipment API fees.
ideas.problem: Carriers generally win accessorial disputes when the service was required and performed, and the burden of proof is on the shipper (dock photos, delivery receipt). Rate-file automation, which is what the big auditors run, cannot tell whether a liftgate was actually used. His own fact-check file states the same limit.
ideas.solution: Address truth from licensed map and parcel data (dock presence, commercial vs residential; do not scrape consumer map products, whose terms forbid it); an SMS to the consignee after delivery ('Was a liftgate used? Was a dock available?'); parse the signed receipt and driver photos; auto-compose the dispute within the carrier's window (some allow only 30 days). Kill test: on 30 real disputed accessorials, at least 40% withdrawn after an evidence packet and at least 30% consignee text response; otherwise shelve it.
ideas.why_now: Accessorials are the highest-value error class in his own research, incumbents cannot verify events, and NMFC and accessorial changes are raising billing friction; cheap SMS, parsing and imagery AI make per-shipment evidence economical for the first time.
ideas.founder_edge: He already shipped the cube-rule and invoice-checker tools and builds SMS-first flows fast; MHC's offices are real consignees to test on; MedFreight clients provide consignee lists.
ideas.first_10_customers: MedFreight clients get it bundled; one DME shop that delivers to homes; two brokers wanting a differentiator; MHC offices as test consignees.
ideas.path_to_big: An API licensed to freight-audit firms, brokers and TMS vendors, priced per shipment, built on a growing address-truth and dispute-outcome dataset. Unproven: carriers may not budge, and consignee response rates are unknown.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nobody found sells consignee-confirmed event evidence. Warp's free tool flags suspicious accessorials by rule; address-classification vendors only classify addresses; SMC3 RateWare Plus (industry-association owned) covers published accessorial rates, not events; the big freight-audit firms check invoice vs rate file.

ideas.title: ProofPack: Medicare proof-of-delivery packets for shipped DME and pharmacy orders
ideas.one_liner: Auto-build the proof-of-delivery file Medicare auditors demand (full carrier tracking, signature, date, recipient) for every shipped order and flag gaps before billing.
ideas.customer: DME/HME suppliers that ship resupply (CPAP, diabetic, wound care) and small pharmacies, starting with any DME or pharmacy arm of MHC; peers through HME buying groups (VGM cites about 3,500 providers and 9,000 locations).
ideas.who_pays: The supplier's owner or compliance lead pays $149-499 a month per location; budget line is audit exposure and recoupments.
ideas.problem: For shipped DMEPOS items the record must trace the item from supplier to beneficiary and be kept 7 years; without it claims are denied and overpayments requested. With 79,000+ enrolled suppliers and an active DME fraud crackdown, small shops with paper tickets and screenshots are exposed.
ideas.solution: Connect to carrier tracking feeds plus an order CSV; generate a per-claim PDF packet; add e-signature delivery tickets for direct deliveries; answer documentation requests in minutes; later monetize the same tracking data with 25% parcel-refund recovery. Sign a BAA, use HIPAA-eligible hosting, minimum-necessary fields keyed by order ID, and get an attorney review.
ideas.why_now: Federal DME crackdown and enrollment moratorium (Feb 27 to Aug 27, 2026) raise audit intensity; carrier tracking APIs make packet assembly cheap.
ideas.founder_edge: Fast build of tracking-to-packet pipelines; MHC as a possible pilot (only if it has a DME or pharmacy arm, which is unverified).
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC's DME or pharmacy arm if any; three HMEs from the family circle; six from a talk to a state association or VGM-type group.
ideas.path_to_big: Evidence layer for every payer that demands proof of delivery, plus refund recovery; 10,000 locations at $250 a month is $30M, but that is a large share of buying-group networks, so it is heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ParcelShield (predictive tracking plus proof-of-delivery audit; Walmart Specialty and UNC Health named), practice-management vendors (Brightree, WellSky workflows), VGM Fulfillment for outsourced fulfilment, parcel refund firms (Refund Retriever, ShipScience). Small shops are underserved but incumbents are well funded.

ideas.title: Advisor-Embedded Leak Check: a white-label spend-leak scan advisors give their business-owner clients
ideas.one_liner: A CPA, RIA or fractional CFO hands a business-owner client a branded leak check (freight, supplier surcharges, duplicate fees) run by the engine; the client pays only on recovery.
ideas.customer: Advisors and CPAs with business-owner clients (channel); the business owners are the end buyers.
ideas.who_pays: The client pays 15-20% of recoveries; the advisor pays nothing at first and later a flat annual license (not per-referral commissions).
ideas.problem: Advisors want retention hooks and cannot see accounts-payable leaks; owners rarely audit freight or supplier surcharges. Referral commissions are a compliance trap (AICPA limits for attest clients, fiduciary conflict disclosure), so the structure must avoid per-referral pay.
ideas.solution: White-label intake portal where the client uploads 12 months of freight bills and supplier invoices; engine runs freight audit and the surcharge ledger; advisor sees a co-branded summary. Use a flat license or no fee so no commission rule is triggered.
ideas.why_now: The tariff-refund and surcharge disputes (idea 1) give advisors a timely reason to call business-owner clients.
ideas.founder_edge: Ron's 24 years in financial services and a network of pre-screened flat-fee advisors; MFA built compliance technology for advisors, so Ron understands how they vet vendors.
ideas.first_10_customers: Three advisors Ron introduces, each bringing two or three business-owner clients, plus three CPAs from the same circle.
ideas.path_to_big: A distribution channel rather than a product; only worth building if ideas 1 or 2 work. Advisors are cautious endorsing third-party vendors, so scale is slow.
ideas.who_does_it_today: FreightWise pays referral commissions to brokers and fulfilment firms; cost-reduction consultancies run franchise-style CPA channels (not verified in detail); tariff-refund firms court CPAs. No white-label leak check for advisors found.

ideas.title: Baygrass Buying Club: an event-production co-op for independent festivals
ideas.one_liner: Independent festivals share anonymized vendor quotes and invoices; the club benchmarks staging, sound, fencing, sanitation and trucking prices, runs pooled bids, and audits invoices against contracts.
ideas.customer: Independent festival directors, starting with bluegrass and Americana festivals, later fairs, races and municipal events.
ideas.who_pays: Festival pays $49-199 a month; vendors pay an administrative fee on pooled deals (the model CAHSAH's purchasing group uses with vendor royalties).
ideas.problem: Stage, sound, lighting, labor and insurance costs jumped. Okeechobee paused future editions after its 2026 return, Michelada Fest cancelled again in 2026 citing production, labor and insurance costs, and UK independent festivals fell from roughly 800-900 to 592 in 2025.
ideas.solution: Shared price database and benchmark per unit (stage hour, fence foot, porta-potty), quarterly pooled RFPs for supplies and rentals, and invoice-versus-contract audit for overages and delivery or fuel fees.
ideas.why_now: Cost squeeze is forcing independents to cancel; pooled buying is the obvious survival tool but no US festival co-op was found.
ideas.founder_edge: Ron co-founded Annapolis Baygrass (IBMA 2026 Event of the Year nominee) and knows the bluegrass circuit; Baygrass is a ready pilot.
ideas.first_10_customers: Baygrass first; then five to nine festivals Ron names through IBMA and regional associations.
ideas.path_to_big: Honest: bluegrass festivals are a small market. Reaching $10M needs a broader temporary-events co-op (fairs, races, municipal events) with about $300M of pooled spend at a 3% fee; plausible only if the first festivals show real savings. The '15-30% pooled discount' claim is an undocumented ticketing-vendor blog claim.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No US festival buying co-op found; UK Association of Independent Festivals offers member benefits; home-care GPOs (HPSI, IMCO, MED Group) prove the GPO model in a neighboring sector.

ideas.title: Broker Audit Drop-In: the audit engine white-labeled to freight brokers, 3PLs and parcel consultants
ideas.one_liner: Brokers with 50-300 small shippers each add 'we audit your bills' as a feature run by his engine and pay per enrolled shipper.
ideas.customer: Independent freight brokers, 3PLs and parcel consultants serving small shippers.
ideas.who_pays: The broker pays $100-300 a month per enrolled shipper or gives a 30% share of recoveries.
ideas.problem: Small shippers do not audit, brokers want differentiation, and building an audit engine is beyond a small broker. Weakness: brokers earn on volume and may not want carrier errors surfaced; no family tie.
ideas.solution: Hosted engine with broker-branded intake, per-shipper reports and a claims queue; brokers keep the client relationship.
ideas.why_now: The engine is built and tested; the NMFC density rewrite and accessorial growth create audit demand; one broker equals many shippers.
ideas.founder_edge: Finished engine and call sheet; speed to onboard; MedFreight results can serve as proof points.
ideas.first_10_customers: Three brokers from the existing call list; any broker serving a MedFreight client; four from freight-association contacts.
ideas.path_to_big: Scale is multiplied by the broker's book, but still capped by small-shipper recoveries; only meaningful if idea 2 proves the engine finds real money.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Freight-audit-and-payment firms (Cass, nVision and others), TMS-embedded audit modules, and FreightWise, which pays referral commissions to brokerages, audit and fulfilment firms.

ideas.title: Cold-Chain Claims Desk: reship and refund recovery for independent specialty and infusion pharmacies
ideas.one_liner: Track every temperature-sensitive overnight parcel, file the carrier's late-delivery refund inside its roughly 15-day window, and document reships and excursions for claims.
ideas.customer: Independent specialty, compounding and infusion pharmacies; any MHC pharmacy or infusion arm as pilot (unverified).
ideas.who_pays: The pharmacy owner pays 25% of refunds and claims recovered.
ideas.problem: Reships after late or distressed cold-chain parcels cost real money; FedEx and UPS money-back guarantees now cover only overnight and 2-day AM services, request windows are about 15 days, and late-eligible volume is about 3.5% of shipments, so monitoring must be continuous. Carrier liability for temperature-sensitive pharma may be limited by tariff (not verified).
ideas.solution: Ingest carrier invoices and tracking, match each late or distressed parcel to its refund eligibility, file inside the window, build excursion evidence for claims, and benchmark packaging and lane failure rates.
ideas.why_now: Direct-to-patient specialty shipments keep growing and carriers narrowed guarantees, so pharmacies leave money unclaimed.
ideas.founder_edge: Fast build of the tracking and filing loop; pharmacy contacts through the family if any.
ideas.first_10_customers: MHC-linked pharmacy if one exists; three independents via a state pharmacy association; six via cold outreach.
ideas.path_to_big: Folds into ProofPack (idea 4) as monetization of the same tracking data; standing alone it is small.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ParcelShield (tracking and intervention, Walmart Specialty and UNC Health), Refund Retriever, ShipScience and LateShipment (refunds), sensor vendors such as SpotSee. Generic parcel refund recovery is crowded.
